title: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure
body: Economist Charles Goodhart observed in 1975 that statistics used to steer policy tend to break down once people start aiming at them, because behaviour shifts to hit the number rather than the goal behind it. The snappy one-line version was popularised by anthropologist Marilyn Strathern in 1997. Examples are everywhere: a call centre judged on call length may rush customers off the phone, and a school judged on test scores may teach to the test.

slides.question: In what year did economist Charles Goodhart first state his law?
slides.explanation: Charles Goodhart made the observation in a 1975 paper on UK monetary policy. Marilyn Strathern’s one-line version, the form everyone quotes, came in 1997.

slides.question: Why does a statistic break down once people aim at it?
options: Behaviour shifts to hit the number
Targets are always set too high
slides.explanation: People chase the number rather than the goal behind it: a call centre judged on call length may rush customers, and a school judged on scores may teach to the test.
